title: Careers and Gap Years
subtitle: A careers fair, a year off, a first job and a volunteer

parts.title: Notices and messages
parts.instructions: For each notice, choose what it means.
notices: CAREERS FAIR: Meet employers from twenty local companies in the school hall on Friday from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Bring a copy of your CV if you have one.
WORK EXPERIENCE: Students in Year 10 will spend two weeks in a workplace in June. Forms must be returned to Mrs Ortega by Friday 12 May.
VOLUNTEERS WANTED: Our animal shelter needs helpers on Saturday mornings. No experience is necessary, and we will give you training.
JOB VACANCY: The Blue Door Café needs a waiter or waitress for weekends. You must be at least sixteen. Ask for the manager, Mr Dunn.
INTERVIEW TIPS: Arrive ten minutes early, wear smart clothes and prepare answers to common questions. Practise with a friend at home.

parts.title: Choosing a career
parts.instructions: Read what each person is looking for. Match each person to the best text. There are three extra texts.

people.text: Pilar loves working with children and is patient and kind. She would like a job where she can help young people to learn and grow.
Anselm is good at drawing and loves computers. He would like to create characters and pictures for video games.
Odette enjoys being outdoors and is very strong. She wants to build houses and see the results of her work.
Kwame is curious about how the body works and wants to look after people who are ill. He is not afraid of hard work.
Lars likes speaking in front of people and is very good at languages. He would like a job that involves travelling to many countries.

texts.title: Teacher
texts.text: Help children to learn new things every day. You need patience and kindness.

texts.title: Chef

texts.title: Journalist

parts.title: A year off
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
When I finished school, everyone expected me to go straight to university. Instead, I decided to take a year off. My parents were worried at first, and my teacher told me that I would forget everything I had learnt. But I wanted to see the world before I chose a career.

For the first four months, I worked in a supermarket to save money. It was not very exciting, and my back hurt from lifting boxes, but I knew it was only for a short time. In January, I flew to Peru, where I spent six months teaching English in a small village school.

The children were wonderful. They arrived early every morning, and they listened carefully to every word I said. After the lessons, we often played football on a dusty field. I learnt Spanish from them far faster than I could have done from a book, and I made friends who I still write to.

When I came home, I felt like a different person. I was more confident, and I knew exactly what I wanted to study: education. Looking back, I do not regret the year for one minute. It was the best decision I have ever made.

options: To see the world before choosing a career
Because he failed his final exams
Because his parents asked him to
questions.explanation: He wanted to see the world before choosing a career.

options: To earn money for his plans
questions.explanation: He worked there to save money.

options: He worked on a farm for a family
He taught English in a village school
He studied Spanish in a language school
questions.explanation: He spent six months teaching English.

questions.prompt: How did he learn Spanish?
questions.explanation: He learnt it from the children.

questions.prompt: How does he feel about the year now?
options: He wishes he had saved more
He thinks it was too long
He is very glad that he did it
questions.explanation: He does not regret it and calls it the best decision.

parts.title: Starting your first job
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
Starting your first job can be exciting and a little frightening at the same time. [1] Everything is new, from the people you meet to the rules you must follow, so it is normal to feel nervous.

On your first day, arrive a little early. [2] Smile, introduce yourself and try to remember people's names, even if it is difficult at first.

Do not be afraid to ask questions. [3] Your colleagues would much prefer that you ask than make a mistake that nobody notices until later.

It is also important to be reliable. [4] If you say that you will finish something by Friday, make sure that you do. Over time, people will learn to trust you. [5] Finally, remember that everybody makes mistakes when they start, and what matters is that you learn from them.
sentences: Nobody expects you to know everything immediately.
This shows your employer that you are serious about the job.
Many people feel this way before the first morning arrives.
You will probably have to fill in some forms.
This is the moment when you make your first impression.
You may need to travel a long way to get there.

gaps.explanation: Feeling this way before the first morning leads to why everything is new.
Arriving early is when you make a first impression, then you smile and introduce yourself.
Nobody expects you to know everything, so do not be afraid to ask questions.
Being reliable shows the employer you are serious, then the example about Friday.
The final advice stays on the first-impression theme: learning from mistakes helps.

parts.title: Job advice
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Choosing a job is one of the most important decisions in life. Many young people feel pressure to decide [1] they are still at school, but it is fine to change your mind. A good way to start is to think about what you enjoy doing most. Do you like working [2] people, or do you prefer to work alone? Are you good [3] solving problems? You can also talk to adults who do jobs that interest you. Ask them what they like [4] their work and what they find difficult. Remember that most people have several different jobs in [5] lives, so you do not need to be perfect from the start. The most important thing is to find something that makes [6] happy.

gaps.explanation: Decide "while" they are still at school.
Most people have jobs in "their" lives.

parts.title: A talk about work experience
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note with one word.

turns.speaker: hilary
turns.text: Good morning, Year Ten. Today I want to explain how work experience will work this summer. You will spend two weeks in a workplace, starting on the fifth of June. You can choose a place yourself, but it must be less than ten kilometres from your home. You should wear smart clothes, and you must arrive on time every day. Most placements are unpaid, but some companies will give you lunch. During the second week, a teacher will visit you to see how you are getting on. At the end, you will write a report of about five hundred words. Before you go, please bring the form that your parents have signed. If you have any questions, come and see me in Room Twelve.

gaps.explanation: Starting on the fifth of June.

gaps.prompt: The workplace must be less than ___ kilometres from home
gaps.explanation: Less than ten kilometres from your home.
Some companies will give you lunch.

gaps.explanation: Come and see me in Room Twelve.

parts.title: A volunteer worker
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: victor
turns.text: Today's guest is Ingrid Solberg, who spent a year working as a volunteer in Africa. Ingrid, what made you go?

turns.speaker: ingrid
turns.text: I had finished my degree, but I didn't feel ready to start a normal job. I wanted to do something useful first.

turns.speaker: victor
turns.text: What kind of work did you do?

turns.speaker: ingrid
turns.text: I helped to build a small clinic in a village. I mixed cement, carried bricks and painted walls. I had never done anything like it.

turns.speaker: victor
turns.text: Was it difficult?

turns.speaker: ingrid
turns.text: Physically, yes, especially in the heat. But the hardest part was missing my family. The internet was slow, so I could only talk to them once a week.

turns.speaker: victor
turns.text: What did you learn?

turns.speaker: ingrid
turns.text: To be patient. Things happen slowly there, but people are generous. They shared their food with us even when they had very little.

turns.speaker: victor
turns.text: How did the year change your plans?

turns.speaker: ingrid
turns.text: Before I left, I was going to be an engineer. Now I want to train as a doctor, so I can work in places like that village.

turns.speaker: victor
turns.text: Would you advise others to do the same?

turns.speaker: ingrid
turns.text: Yes, if they can. But choose a project carefully, and talk to people who have been there before.
